title: Jaipur
wiki_lead:
Jaipur (Rajasthani: Jayapura, pronounced [ˈd͡ʑɛpʊɾᵊ]) is the capital and largest city of the north-western Indian state of Rajasthan. As of 2011, the city had a population of 3.1 million, making it the tenth-most populous city in the country. Located 268 km (167 mi) from the national capital, New Delhi, Jaipur is also known as the Pink City due to the dominant colour scheme of its buildings in the old city.
Jaipur was founded in 1727 by Sawai Jai Singh II, the Kachhwaha Rajput ruler of Amer, after whom the city was named. It is one of the earliest planned cities of modern India, designed by Vidyadhar Bhattacharya. During the British colonial period, the city served as the capital of the princely state of Jaipur. After Indian independence in 1947, Jaipur became the capital of the newly formed state of Rajasthan in 1949.
Jaipur is a popular tourist destination in India, forming a part of the Golden Triangle tourist circuit along with Delhi and Agra. The city serves as a gateway to other tourist destinations in Rajasthan, such as Jodhpur, Jaisalmer, Bikaner, Udaipur, Bundi, Kota, and Mount Abu. The historic city center was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List on 6 July 2019, joining the Jantar Mantar (inscribed in 2010) and the nearby Amer Fort (part of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan). The city has colloquially been referred to as the "Paris of India", and Nobel laureate C. V. Raman described it as the "Island of Glory".

Etymology
Jaipur derives its name from Sawai Jai Singh II, the Kachhwaha ruler of Amer, who founded the city in 1727. In Sanskrit, variations of the suffix -pur or -pura denote a city or town; thus, "Jaipur" translates to "The City of Jai" or "Jai's City".


History

Jaipur was founded on 18 November 1727 by Jai Singh II, the Kachhwaha Rajput ruler of Amer, who ruled the region from 1699 to 1743. He planned to shift his capital 11 km (7 mi) from Amer to accommodate a growing population and increasing water scarcity. Jai Singh consulted several architects and planned the city based on the principles of Vastu Shastra and Shilpa Shastra, under the architectural guidance of Vidyadhar Bhattacharya. The construction of the city began in 1726. During the rule of Sawai Ram Singh II, the city was painted pink to welcome Albert Edward, Prince of Wales in 1876. Many of the avenues remain painted in pink, giving Jaipur a distinctive appearance and the epithet "Pink City".
In the 19th century, the city grew rapidly, reaching a population of 160,000 by 1900. The wide boulevards were paved, and its chief industries included metalwork and marble, fostered by a school of art founded in 1868. In August 1981, large areas of the city, including the airport, were flooded following heavy rains from a cloudburst, resulting in eight deaths and extensive damage along the Dravyavati River. On 6 July 2019, the city was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.


Geography


Topography
Jaipur is located in the eastern Rajasthan and covers a total area of 467 km2 (180 sq mi). The terrain generally slopes downwards from north to south and towards the southeast. The city is bordered by fertile alluvial plains to the east and south, while the northern and western margins feature hill chains and arid areas. The Aravalli range bounds the city, with the Nahargarh hills to the north and the Jhalana hills to the east.
The Dravyavati River serves as the city's primary drainage channel; however, by 2014, it had degenerated into an untreated sewage drain. To address this issue, a rejuvenation plan was developed by the Jaipur Development Authority (JDA) in 2015. A 13 km (8.1 mi) stretch of Dravyavati riverfront out of 47.5 km (29.5 mi) was opened following restoration in 2018, with the remaining project was completed in 2022.

Renowned as the Pink City for its buildings painted in terracotta pinkâa color symbolizing hospitality âsince 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales, Jaipur exemplifies early modern urban planning with grid layouts, wide avenues, and fortified walls integrating Rajput, Mughal, and later European architectural influences. In 2019, its walled core was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site for outstanding universal value in criteria including cultural exchange and exemplary town planning. The city anchors Rajasthan 's tourism economy, drawing visitors to landmarks like the Hawa Mahal facade, Jantar Mantar astronomical observatory, and nearby Amber Fort, while serving as a hub for jewelry, textiles, and information technology industries amid a metropolitan population exceeding four million.
